subject: chemistry
title: Purity, formulations and chromatography
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Purity, formulations and chromatography — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.8.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Purity, formulations and chromatography, specification section 4.8.1.
final_note: You worked through Purity, formulations and chromatography — 17 specification statements.

concepts.def: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Purity is about what the sample contains, not about where it came from or how clean it looks.
Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. A mixture is not a pure substance, however carefully it has been made and however uniform it looks.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes between solid and liquid. A pure substance melts at one temperature, and that value can be compared with accepted data.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes between liquid and gas. A pure substance boils at one temperature under fixed conditions.

concepts.term: Melting or boiling over a range
concepts.def: A mixture does not melt or boil at one specific temperature; the change happens over a range of temperatures. A measured range, rather than a single sharp value, is the evidence that a sample is a mixture and not a pure substance.

In everyday language, a pure substance can mean a substance that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk. Such a product is usually a mixture in the chemical sense.
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose.
Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Changing the quantities changes how the product behaves.
Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. They can be solid, liquid or gaseous products.
A separation method that can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances.
The phase in a chromatography experiment that does not move. In paper chromatography the stationary phase is the paper.
The phase that moves through the stationary phase, carrying substances with it. In paper chromatography the mobile phase is the solvent moving up the paper.

Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases. A substance that spends more of its time in the mobile phase is carried further up the paper; one held more strongly by the stationary phase moves less far.
The finished paper, showing the pencil origin line, the marked solvent front and the separated spots. It is interpreted by counting spots and by measuring distances to calculate Rf values.
The pencil line on which the spots are placed at the start. All distances moved by a substance are measured from this line to the centre of its spot.
The furthest point reached by the solvent, marked as soon as the paper is taken out. The distance moved by the solvent is measured from the origin to this line.

The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent. It is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no units, and because a substance cannot travel further than the solvent that carries it, its value lies between 0 and 1.
Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent. Both distances are measured in the same unit, from the origin line.

The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent, but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents. One spot in one solvent alone is therefore not proof of purity.

Investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances, calculating Rf values. The origin line is drawn in pencil, the solvent starts below that line, the paper is removed before the solvent reaches the top and the solvent front is marked at once.

An Rf value is quoted to no more significant figures than the measurements it came from. Distances read to the nearest millimetre give two significant figures, so an Rf value is normally given to two significant figures rather than to all the digits on the calculator.

mcqs.q: In chemistry, which of these samples counts as a pure substance?
options: Spring water sold as natural, with nothing added to it
Sea water, because water and salt are both pure chemicals
Clean air, because its gases are clear and dry throughout
Distilled water, a single compound with nothing else in it
mcqs.explain: A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.

mcqs.q: A student says a compound cannot be pure because it contains more than one element. What is wrong with this?
options: A compound is one substance, so a compound alone is pure
Nothing is wrong, since only elements can be classed as pure
A compound is pure only if just two elements are combined
A compound is pure only if it was made in a laboratory
mcqs.explain: The specification counts a single element or a single compound as pure; the number of elements combined is irrelevant.

mcqs.q: Four solid samples were heated gently. Which result shows a pure substance?
options: It melted steadily between 65 and 79 degrees C as it warmed
It melted at 80 degrees C, with no change over a range
It melted between 78 and 82 degrees C, close to the true value
It melted at 80 degrees C after softening from 70 degrees C
mcqs.explain: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so melting at one fixed value is the evidence of purity.

mcqs.q: Liquid A boils steadily at 100 degrees C. Liquid B starts boiling at 97 degrees C and the temperature rises to 103 degrees C. What can be concluded?
options: A is a pure substance and B is a mixture
Both are pure, but B was heated too quickly
B is pure, since it boiled near 100 degrees C
A is a mixture, as it boiled at one temperature
mcqs.explain: A pure liquid boils at a specific temperature; a boiling range shows that B is a mixture.

mcqs.q: A carton is labelled 'pure milk'. What does the label mean?
options: Nothing has been added; chemically the milk is a mixture
The milk is a single compound, so it is chemically pure
The milk is pure because it is white with nothing in it
The milk is pure because each substance in it is pure
mcqs.explain: This is the everyday meaning given in the specification: unadulterated and in its natural state, though chemically milk is a mixture.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?
options: Any mixture of two or more substances, however it was made
A liquid in which several solids have been fully dissolved
A pure compound made by reacting measured amounts together
A mixture designed as a useful product, in measured quantities
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition: a mixture designed as a useful product, mixed in carefully measured quantities.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a formulation?
options: Muddy river water, a mixture of soil, water and dissolved salts
Paint, mixed from pigment, binder and solvent in set amounts
Copper, a pure metal drawn into wire for electrical wiring
Sodium chloride, a compound added to food in measured amounts
mcqs.explain: Paint is named in the specification's list and is a mixture whose components are measured to give the required properties.

mcqs.q: A product label lists five ingredients, each with a percentage and a stated job such as cleaning, thickening or perfuming. What does this show?
options: It is a pure substance, since every ingredient is listed
It is a formulation, as each measured part has a purpose
It is a compound, because the parts are in fixed amounts
It is a formulation only if the product is a medicine
mcqs.explain: Components in measured quantities, each with a particular purpose, is exactly what identifies a formulation.

mcqs.q: Why is brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, described as a formulation?
options: It is not one, because formulations must be liquid products
Its metals combine chemically in a fixed ratio when melted
Its metals are mixed in measured amounts for useful properties
It is not one, because alloys are only studied as metals
mcqs.explain: Alloys are in the specification's list of formulations, and the proportions are chosen to give the required properties.

mcqs.q: In paper chromatography, which statement about the phases is correct?
options: The solvent is the stationary phase and the paper is mobile
The spots are the stationary phase and the paper is mobile
The paper is the stationary phase and the spots are mobile
The paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is mobile
mcqs.explain: The paper does not move; the solvent travels through it carrying the substances.

mcqs.q: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?
options: The lightest particles are carried furthest up the paper
Substances held most strongly by the paper travel furthest
They are distributed differently between the two phases
Each substance travels a distance fixed by its own colour
mcqs.explain: The specification states that separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.

mcqs.q: Which substance in a mixture moves furthest up the paper?
options: The one with the smallest and lightest particles in the mixture
The one held most strongly by the paper it soaks through
The one most attracted to the solvent and least to the paper
The one placed on the pencil line in the largest single spot
mcqs.explain: Spending more time in the mobile phase and less held by the stationary phase carries a substance furthest.

mcqs.q: Which expression gives the Rf value of a substance?
options: distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance
distance moved by substance / total length of the paper
distance moved by solvent / distance left above the spot
distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
mcqs.explain: This is the equation exactly as the specification states it.

mcqs.q: When finding how far a substance has moved on a chromatogram, where is the distance measured?
options: From the pencil line to the centre of the spot
From the pencil line to the top edge of the spot
From the bottom of the paper to the spot's centre
From the base of the spot up to the solvent front
mcqs.explain: The specification specifies the centre of the spot measured from the origin.

mcqs.q: On a chromatogram the centre of a spot is 3.6 cm from the pencil line, and the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the pencil line. What is the Rf value of the substance?
options: 4.4 cm
mcqs.explain: 3.6 / 8.0 = 0.45, a ratio with no units, given to two significant figures.

mcqs.q: A spot moved 34 mm and the solvent moved 75 mm, both measured to the nearest millimetre. How should the Rf value be given?
mcqs.explain: Both measurements have two significant figures, so the Rf value is quoted to two significant figures.

mcqs.q: Why can the same compound have a different Rf value in a different solvent?
options: It cannot, because each compound has one fixed Rf value
Its distribution between the phases changes with the solvent
In a new solvent the paper always holds the compound more
The compound moves further than the solvent in some liquids
mcqs.explain: Rf depends on how the compound is shared between that particular solvent and the paper, so a new solvent gives a new value.

mcqs.q: A sample gives one spot when run in a single solvent. What can be concluded?
options: It is definitely pure, because only one spot developed
It is the same compound as every sample giving one spot
It may be pure; it must give one spot in all solvents
Nothing follows, because no Rf value has been calculated
mcqs.explain: The specification requires a single spot in all solvents before a compound is taken to be pure.

mcqs.q: Which chromatography result is evidence that a sample is impure?
options: It separated into three spots when one solvent was used
It gave a single spot in each of three different solvents
Its single spot had the same Rf value as a known dye
Its single spot had a much larger area than the others
mcqs.explain: More than one spot shows more than one compound is present, so the sample is a mixture.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 6, why is the line on which the spots are placed drawn in pencil?
options: A pen line works too if the ink is a different colour
A pencil line can be drawn far more thinly than ink
Pencil does not dissolve, so the line stays in place
Ink would react chemically with the dyes in the spots
mcqs.explain: Graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so the origin line does not run and the measurements stay valid.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 6, why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line?
options: Otherwise the solvent cannot dissolve the spots at all
Otherwise the solvent would rise up the paper too fast
Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent and are lost
Otherwise the solvent front could not be marked at the end
mcqs.explain: Spots below the surface dissolve into the pool instead of travelling up the paper, so nothing separates.

mcqs.q: A known dye X has an Rf value of 0.62 in a solvent. A mixture run in the same solvent gives spots at Rf 0.31, 0.62 and 0.85. What follows?
options: The mixture is dye X, since one spot has the same Rf value
The mixture cannot contain X, because X gives only one spot
The mixture contains X, and the other spots are the solvent
The mixture may contain X, along with two other compounds
mcqs.explain: A matching Rf value in the same solvent is information that helps identify a compound, and the other two spots are further compounds.

mcqs.q: What can paper chromatography do for a mixture of coloured substances?
options: Separate it and give information helping to identify parts
Name every substance in it without using any known samples
Show how much of each substance the mixture contains
Split each substance in it into the elements it contains
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification claims for chromatography: separation, plus information that helps identification.
